title: An Astute SNL Sketch About Who Deals With Aging Parents
text:
Like a lot of Millennials coming to terms with the inevitability of elder care, John Mulaney is thinking about Baby Boomers. The aging generation came up throughout last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live , the 44-year-old Mulaney’s seventh as host. He teased Boomers in his monologue, claiming that all of the complaints they have about Gen Z are actually true of Boomers: They, too, are addicted to technology, behave toxically online, and melt down when they feel ignored.

 Continuing the ribbing, one sketch portrayed a group of younger Boomers at Woodstock; Mulaney’s character, bedecked in a frizzy wig and a brown fringe jacket, imagined the houses and money they could amass in the future. “I feel like we should get as much of it as we can and then just, like, have it,” he said, to the confusion of his weed-smoking hippie friends. (Yes, it was a very on-the-nose bit about how Boomers left their flower-power ideals in the 1960s.)

 But Mulaney’s motif played out most effectively in the pretaped sketch “Sister.” This spoof on a pharmaceutical ad proposes a solution to the problem of finding high-quality care for elderly parents : “I didn’t know where to turn,” a smug Mulaney says of his trouble helping his father. “That’s when I heard about Sister”—Mulaney’s character’s actual sister, that is. After “years of internalized sexism” warping her brain, the ad notes, a simple text message will compel Sister to leave her life behind for the responsibility of live-in, unpaid, around-the-clock care. The tendency of older female siblings to take on practical and emotional labor in their family unit has become an observable phenomenon in social-science research, and something of a meme too. In the sketch, as in life, they need not even be the eldest—societal pressures on women can work on daughters generally.

 The sketch was pointed about the fact that children can love their ailing parents without loving the extra work of elder care—especially when it means navigating complex systems such as health care. “Speak to human. Speak to human ,” a Sister, portrayed by Jane Wickline, says forcefully into a phone. Those tasks can be difficult for anyone—but some people pawn them off on siblings. “I used to get overwhelmed by my dad’s medications,” says Kenan Thompson’s character, but it’s not a problem for Sister—or, if it is, she hasn’t brought it up.

 The sketch highlights not just the central unfairness of women taking on this kind of care work but the hurtful resentments that build over time in these situations. The father in the ad comments on his daughter’s weight out of the blue and complains about her control of his salt intake. Sister’s husband can also be looped into the work, but when he asks about why they had to upend their lives, Sister’s reply is forceful: “Because he’s my dad, that’s why!”

 [ Read: The parenting prophecy ] 

 Judging from the attention the sketch is getting this morning, its portrayal of a growing elderly population’s strain on many families resonated with viewers. If you listen closely, the sketch offers a solution of sorts: A disclaimer at the end of the ad says that the offer on Sister is void if she “has a good therapist.”

 Mulaney got more specific about a Boomer in his own life during his monologue. He discussed how deciding his father is autistic has “cleared up everything about our childhoods”—even explaining behaviors such as shaking hands with a baby or trying to make small talk about the fullness of a trash can (with a 4-year-old).

 One notable Baby Boomer with a penchant for rambling tangents was absent from this week’s SNL : Donald Trump. The cold open instead riffed on Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Mulaney’s CIA officer tried to warn tech billionaires such as Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane) about the dangers of honey traps, insisting that there was no overlap between their interests and those of beautiful women. Those guys are not Boomers—the youngest, Sam Altman (played here by Ben Marshall), is 41—but in the sketch, they didn’t seem to be able to understand the lesson. Every generation has its shortcomings.
